extracted.intended_audience: authors of healthcare quality improvement (QI) / improvement science reports (manuscript authors preparing SQUIRE-compliant reports)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and reporting healthcare quality improvement/intervention studies so readers can understand interventions, context, outcomes, and ethical considerations and judge reproducibility and generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics approval and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports should explicitly describe how potential ethical concerns were reviewed and addressed in development and implementation of the intervention, including whether independent review occurred (eg, research ethics committee, facility quality management office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations vary between countries and institutions; state clearly what review mechanism was used (research ethics committee, quality management office, etc.) and provide details of approvals (committee name, reference/approval number) where applicable. This assures readers that ethical implications were considered in design, implementation and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing interests / conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should provide clear and detailed information concerning any potential conflicts of interest or competing interests related to the improvement work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report employment relationships, royalty agreements, advisory roles, reimbursements, shareholders, or other ties to products/organisations involved in the work. State presence or absence of conflicts under a labeled heading (eg, 'Competing Interests').

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: evolution of the intervention and details of process measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the initial steps of the intervention(s) and their evolution over time (eg, timeline diagram, flow chart or table), including modifications made to the intervention during the project, and provide details of the process measures and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present interventions by phase if applicable (eg, phases I–III, sustainability) and explain why they evolved and how roles were impacted. Include specific process measures (eg, percent receiving antibiotics within 60 minutes) and outcome measures; allow readers to imagine adaptation in their context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report implementation fidelity / degree of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the degree of success achieved in implementing an intervention (fidelity), for example the proportion of the intervention actually delivered as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express fidelity quantitatively where possible (eg, percentage of eligible patients for whom the intervention was performed). Use these measures to assess how thoroughly the intervention was implemented and to interpret outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of annotated charts and statistical process control (SPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use control charts or other time-series plots annotated with intervention phases to show changes in process/outcome measures over time and to illustrate where each intervention fits relative to results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate charts with phases/interventions to enable readers to see timing and sustainment of effects; present charts that show both improvement and changes in variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: contextual elements that interacted with interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe contextual elements that interacted with the interventions (structural variables such as organisational/practice type, volume, payer mix, electronic health record use, geographical location, leadership, organisational structure, data infrastructure, motivation to change, team leadership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide descriptive information about structural/contextual features and how they might have influenced implementation and outcomes. Use tables or text to make associations between context and results clear to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: observed associations between outcomes, interventions and contextual factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Report observed associations between outcomes, the interventions implemented, and relevant contextual factors, including quantitative associations when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present analyses (tables, ORs, CIs) linking leadership, engagement, or other contextual metrics to clinical/process outcomes or to implementation success. Explain how inclusion of other variables affects associations (eg, mediators/reducers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: unintended consequences (benefits, harms, unexpected results, problems or failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report unintended consequences of the intervention such as benefits, harms, unexpected results, problems or failures associated with the intervention(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about negative results or harms as well as benefits; this information is crucial for readers considering replication or adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative and qualitative results (mixed methods reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present both quantitative and qualitative results when used (eg, improvement percentages, odds ratios; focus group themes, interviews) and describe how mixed methods enhanced understanding of context and mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative data to show magnitude/trends and qualitative data to explain mechanisms/leadership/themes. Mixed methods are not required but can deepen interpretation—describe measurement instruments and how qualitative themes were derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: missing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide details about missing data, including why data are missing (technical problems, attrition, lost to follow-up), efforts made to recover data, and any available details about the missing cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting for missing data enables readers to understand potential biases. State numbers and reasons, describe recovery efforts (eg, chart review, outreach attempts) and report how missingness may affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion: focused summary linking findings to aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the discussion with a focused summary of the key findings, including their relevance to the original rationale and specific aims, and the project’s particular strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary should be concise and set up the interpretive discussion rather than restating all results; include distinction of strengths and distinctive features of the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: nature of association and comparison with literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the nature of the association between intervention(s) and outcomes and compare findings with results from other publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss possible mechanisms, compare concordance or discordance with prior studies, and use literature to situate the findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: impact on people and systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the impact of the project on people and systems (eg, culture change, staff roles, workload implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete examples of how the intervention affected staff, patients, or organisational processes and any measurable system-level consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: reasons for differences and role of context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain reasons for any differences between observed and anticipated outcomes, including the influence of contextual factors and opportunity (eg, secular trends, concurrent initiatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer plausible alternative explanations (eg, heightened awareness, prior experience) and discuss how context may have confounded or mediated observed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: costs and strategic trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss costs and strategic trade-offs associated with the intervention and its implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe resource requirements, personnel, leadership buy-in, informatics needs, or other barriers that could limit replication or sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: generalisability and threats to internal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state limits to the generalisability of the work and factors that might have limited internal validity (imprecision, confounding, bias, measurement or analytic limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about which contextual or design features limit applicability elsewhere (eg, tertiary care setting, prior improvement culture). Describe known measurement limitations (eg, lack of validated tools) and how they affect confidence in findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: efforts to minimise and adjust for limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe efforts made to minimise and adjust for limitations (eg, double independent reviews, statistical adjustments, data recovery attempts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain mitigations employed and assess how well they reduce bias or uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions: usefulness, sustainability, spread, implications and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude with statements about the usefulness of the work, its sustainability, potential for spread to other contexts, implications for practice and further study, and suggested next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw practical implications for administrators and practitioners (eg, nurse staffing implications), discuss sustainability dependencies (eg, frontline worker capacity), and suggest concrete next steps for research or implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place evolution of the intervention in Results (mechanism in Methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the mechanism by which interventions were intended to work in the methods section, but place the resulting transformation/evolution of the intervention over time in the results section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation helps readers understand the initial rationale and then observe how interventions actually changed and produced outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient detail to enable replication and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Give detailed descriptions (tables, figures, roles, timelines) of interventions and how staff roles were impacted so readers can imagine adaptation in their own institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify who did what, when, and how; include phase descriptions, role changes, and process maps so others can judge feasibility and adapt interventions to their context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent reporting of negative results and small effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report negative findings, small effect sizes, or seemingly minor improvements and explain their practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why small changes may still be important (eg, small BMI gains), and ensure negative or null findings and limited numbers of events are reported transparently to inform others.
